notes.meaning: Peter and John walked up to the temple courts at three in the afternoon, which was the usual time for afternoon prayer. Even after Jesus rose from the dead, His apostles continued joining their fellow Jews for public prayer to God. Going to the temple at this busy hour also gave them a great opportunity to share the good news about Jesus.

A man who had been unable to walk since birth was carried every day to the temple gate called Beautiful. Because he could not work, his friends placed him where crowds of worshipers passed by, hoping their religious duty would lead them to give him money. His lifelong lameness was well known to everyone, proving that his condition was real and impossible to fake.

When the lame man saw Peter and John about to walk into the temple courts, he called out and begged them for money. He did not know who they were or what they could do, so he expected nothing more than a small coin to help him survive another day.

Peter and John stopped and fixed their eyes directly on the beggar, and Peter told him to look at them. People often ignored beggars, but the apostles wanted the man's full attention. This prepared the man to realize that God was about to do something special through them.

The man looked closely at Peter and John, expecting to receive a gift of money from them. His mind was set only on his physical poverty. He had no idea that God was about to give him something far greater than coins.

Peter told the man plainly that he had no silver or gold coins to give away. Instead, he offered the spiritual help he had received from God by commanding the man to walk in the authority and power of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. By using the humble title 'of Nazareth,' Peter showed that the crucified Jesus is alive and rules with divine power.

Peter took the man by his right hand and helped him up off the ground. In that very instant, God put supernatural strength into the man's weak feet and ankle bones. The healing happened right away, enabling limbs that had never worked before to bear his full weight.

The man leaped straight up onto his feet and began walking around on his own. He followed Peter and John into the temple courts, jumping for joy and shouting praises to God. His leaping fulfilled the ancient promise in Isaiah that the lame would leap like a deer when God comes to save.

All the worshipers in the temple courts saw the man walking around and openly praising God. The miracle was not performed in a dark corner, but in broad daylight in front of the whole public gathering.

The crowd recognized that this energetic man was the exact same beggar who had sat at the Beautiful Gate for decades. Knowing his long history of being crippled, the people were filled with total shock and amazement at what had happened to him.

The healed man held tightly onto Peter and John, expressing his love and deep gratitude to them. Seeing this sight, an astonished crowd quickly ran together to the covered walkway known as Solomon's Colonnade, giving Peter an eager audience.

When Peter saw the excited crowd, he asked the men of Israel why this healing surprised them so much. He warned them not to stare at him and John as if their own human power or personal godliness had cured the man. True servants of God never take credit for miracles, but always point people to the Lord.

Peter declared that the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had brought glory to His Servant Jesus through this miracle. He boldly reminded the crowd that they had handed Jesus over to death and disowned Him before the Roman governor Pilate, even after Pilate wanted to set Him free. Peter used the names of Israel's founding fathers to prove that the apostles were not teaching a new religion, but honoring Israel's true God.

The people of Israel had rejected Jesus, who was pure, innocent, and perfectly righteous before God. In His place, they begged the authorities to grant them Barabbas, a dangerous and guilty murderer. Peter pointed out this terrible contrast to help them see how deeply they had sinned.

The crowd had killed the very Author and Prince of life, but God overturned their wicked act by raising Him back to life. Peter and John announced that they were personal eyewitnesses who had seen the risen Christ alive with their own eyes.

Peter explained that it was faith in the name and authority of Jesus that gave this beggar full health and strong limbs. The crowd knew the man well, so they could easily verify that the complete cure was genuine. Peter made sure everyone knew that this healing came entirely from Jesus, who gives faith and works through it.

differ.view: Some Pentecostal teachers believe the healed man himself exercised faith to receive his cure, while other evangelicals understand the faith as belonging to the apostles or as a direct work of God's grace.

notes.meaning: Peter called his listeners brothers and kindly acknowledged that they and their rulers had acted in ignorance. They did not understand that Jesus was truly their promised Messiah when they sent Him to the cross. Although ignorance did not erase their guilt, it showed that their crime was not hopeless and that God was still ready to forgive them.

Peter explained that God used their sinful choices to fulfill what all the ancient prophets had predicted about the Messiah's suffering. Human rulers could not ruin God's master plan for salvation. God turned their terrible deed into the means of saving sinners through the sacrifice of Christ.

Peter urged the people to repent, meaning they should change their minds and turn back to God so their sins could be completely wiped away. God promises to blot out their record of guilt like wiping ink cleanly off a page. Turning to the Lord also brings times of spiritual refreshment, comfort, and peace straight from God's presence.

differ.view: Some evangelicals teach that the times of refreshing refer specifically to the earthly kingdom that would have begun if Israel had repented as a nation, while others see it as the spiritual peace and renewal believers enjoy throughout the church age.

notes.meaning: If they would repent, God would send Jesus, the Messiah who had been appointed and promised for them from the start. Jesus had already come to die for their sins, and God promised His blessings to all who would welcome Him. For those who believe, the coming of the Lord brings great joy rather than fearful judgment.

differ.view: Some dispensational evangelicals hold that Peter was offering the immediate return of Christ to set up His earthly thousand-year reign if the Jewish nation repented, while other traditions understand this as Christ's ongoing spiritual presence now and His final return on the last day.

notes.meaning: Jesus must stay in the glory of heaven until the final time comes when God restores all things and puts the world right again. His physical body is in heaven, so His followers must now live by faith while looking forward to His return. On that final day, God will complete every good promise He spoke through His holy prophets from the beginning of time.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular modern teachers take the restoration of all things to mean that every human being will eventually be saved and welcomed into heaven, though traditional commentaries limit this to the fulfillment of what the biblical prophets predicted.

notes.meaning: Peter quoted Moses, who had promised Israel that the Lord God would raise up a special prophet like him from among their own people. Moses ordered the people to listen carefully and obey everything this future Prophet would say. Peter showed that Jesus is that supreme Prophet, who speaks the final and perfect truth of God.

Moses warned that anyone who refuses to obey this coming Prophet will be completely cut off from God's people. Rejecting Jesus means rejecting God's own voice, which leads to total spiritual ruin. Peter used the words of Israel's favorite lawgiver to show his hearers how dangerous it was to ignore Christ.

Peter added that every prophet from the time of Samuel onward had spoken about these very days of the Messiah. The prophets formed a long line of witnesses who agreed that a new and better age of salvation was coming. The crowd was now living in the days those prophets had long anticipated.

Peter reminded his Jewish listeners that they were the heirs of the prophets and of the covenant God made with their forefathers. In that covenant, God promised Abraham that through his offspring all families across the earth would be blessed. Because Jesus was born into their nation as that promised offspring, the Jewish people were the first to hear and receive these blessings.

When God raised up and commissioned His Servant Jesus, He sent Him first to the Jewish people to bring them His highest blessing. That blessing was not political power or freedom from Rome, but the saving work of turning each person away from their sins. Christ truly blesses people by forgiving them and giving them the power to live holy lives.
